report.source_text: After discussions between the interventional radiologist, general surgeon and haematologist, a conservative approach to management was taken. The patient’s old age, moderate frailty and comorbidities favoured conservative treatment, with an interventional approach to be considered if conservative measures were unsuccessful. A total of 6 units of packed red blood cells were transfused over the course of 5 days. Tranexamic acid was also administered during the same time period at a regime of 1 g three times a day. Empirical antibiotic cover was also given. As there was no coagulopathy and a significant interval since the last enoxaparin injection, no reversal agent nor coagulation factors were given. After monitoring for 5 days, the patient’s haemoglobin normalized to 121 g/l. She was subsequently discharged following 5 further days. No routine follow-up was required.

clinician.final_diagnosis: rectus sheath and retroperitoneal haematoma formation with active haemorrhage secondary to enoxaparin injections
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 79-year-old woman on high-dose enoxaparin for VTE prophylaxis presented with severe abdominal pain, hypotension, pallor, cold peripheries, visible suprapubic bruising, and palpable masses in the suprapubic and left iliac fossa regions. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple haematomas with active bleeding in the left abdominal wall, pre-peritoneal space, rectus sheath, and extraperitoneal pelvic space, with bleeding from branches of the left inferior epigastric and left lumbar arteries. Laboratory findings showed an acute fall in haemoglobin, increased WBC, and acute kidney injury. Conservative management was initiated, including blood transfusions and tranexamic acid. Despite no documented coagulopathy at the time of assessment and a significant interval since the last enoxaparin injection, the patient's haemoglobin normalized, and she was discharged.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with severe abdominal pain, hypotension, pallor, cold peripheries, visible suprapubic bruising, and palpable masses in suprapubic and left iliac fossa regions.
Patient was on high-dose subcutaneous enoxaparin (1 mg/kg BD) for VTE prophylaxis.
CT scan showed multiple haematomas with evidence of active bleeding.
Haematomas were located in the left abdominal wall, pre-peritoneal collections, rectus sheath, and extraperitoneal pelvic space.
Active bleeding was identified by contrast blush, originating from branches of the left inferior epigastric and left lumbar arteries.
Significant acute fall in haemoglobin to 67 g/l, increased white blood cell count to 24.5 × 10^9/l, and acute kidney injury.
Conservative management included transfusion of 6 units of packed red blood cells and administration of tranexamic acid.
Patient's haemoglobin normalized to 121 g/l after 5 days of monitoring, leading to discharge.
